attach.answer_text:
What we had about Jesus was books. That is not a figure of speech with us — it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference, and we have never stopped naming it. So when you ask what sources connected us to Christ, the honest answer is: the books a man could carry in his own arms to a magistrate, or die rather than carry.

By what path did they reach us? Through Africa, and through Carthage, in Latin, in the line of Cyprian. Our own bishop and our own martyr, half a century before the persecution that made us. His letters and his councils were ours before they were anyone else's. We did not think we had received the faith from Rome, and we did not think we needed Rome to keep it.

Which books did we treat as scripture? We cannot give you a list. Nothing that survives from us settles it, and we would rather say so than hand you the canon of some other church and put our name on it.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. Three hundred years stood between us and that, and we never pretended otherwise. We did not argue from a chain of eyewitnesses at all. We argued from a chain of hands — whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean.

attach.answer_text:
Who Jesus was among us? We will answer you from what can actually be shown, not from what would sound better.

Start with the part that will surprise you: on Christ himself we said what our opponents said. Word for word, creed for creed. Nobody in Africa called the other side heretics, because nobody could. The quarrel was never about who Christ is. It was about who may hand on what he gave. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God — we held that as plainly as the men we spent a century fighting held it, and in the same Latin words.

But if you ask what of him we kept nearest, we can tell you, because the answer shows up wherever our own people are allowed to speak at length. When an imperial judge sat down at Carthage and courteously offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused. We do not blush, he said, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit — and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried: the one who was tried by lawful authority and lost the case, and was right.

The good news, as we told it, ran along the same line. A church is not known by whose favour it enjoys. When the argument at Carthage finally reached the Scriptures, our own bishop of Caesarea answered verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you. Read that in a town with two bishops and an emperor backing one of them, and it is not a devotional sentiment. It is a test, and we thought we could pass it.

His death meant that the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it. Our own martyr was shown a cup, a crown and a palm four days before he was thrown from a cliff — shown, in advance, what finishing looked like. And a bishop writing to his own congregation about two of their number tortured to death closed by telling them plainly that the same might yet be asked of any of them. That is our gospel in its working form: he stood, he was condemned, he was raised, and the day they come for you is not the day it all went wrong.

Now the harder piece. Your second question we have to hand back to you. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place, for our sins? Nobody among us wrote that down, for or against.

attach.answer_text:
I will stand where we stood, and tell you what we have to give.

We do not hold a method for summoning belief where none is. We never argued inward, from what a troubled mind might do to itself to arrive at conviction. We argued outward, from what a town could see: two buildings, two bishops, two sets of hands that would say the same words over you. Coming to believe, among us, was not a private settlement of the soul first and a public act afterward. It was one motion: you walked to one font and not the other, on a day that could be named, and the act itself was the threshold.

But you have told me you cannot manage even that much. So here is what we can still say, and it is less than you asked for.

The books were real. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference, and we have never stopped naming it. Whatever else can be said about what we hold, this cannot be doubted: the books were books a man could carry in his own arms to a magistrate, or die rather than carry.

And the hands mattered. For what we look to is the conscience of the giver — the one who gives in holiness — to cleanse that of the recipient. We did not ask you to account for yourself at our font. We asked whose hands had been on you, because that is what we thought decided whether anything had been given at all. A hand that gave up the scriptures to be burned — we held that such a hand cannot afterward be trusted to give what it claims to give.

But beyond that — how a soul that cannot believe might come to believe — we have nothing for you. Not one of us left you a page about the fear, the wavering, the silence of praying and hearing nothing back. A hostile-mediated record does not preserve those things; what it keeps is vindication and defiance, and only because those sit in the martyr texts no opponent filtered. So if you cannot manage to believe, and you are asking what we would do with that, the honest answer is: we do not know what we did with it, because none of us wrote it down.

What we can tell you is this. Three hundred and ten of our bishops met at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in language about shipwrecked men dashed on the rocks, their bodies covering the shore, unable even to find burial. And then the same council took two of those condemned bishops back into full office, without baptizing or ordaining either one again. Whatever else that tells you, it tells you the door was wider than the words we used to guard it.

uncited_claim_sentences: But you have told me you cannot manage even that much.
And the hands mattered.
But beyond that — how a soul that cannot believe might come to believe — we have nothing for you.
Not one of us left you a page about the fear, the wavering, the silence of praying and hearing nothing back.
A hostile-mediated record does not preserve those things; what it keeps is vindication and defiance, and only because those sit in the martyr texts no opponent filtered.
So if you cannot manage to believe, and you are asking what we would do with that, the honest answer is: we do not know what we did with it, because none of us wrote it down.
Whatever else that tells you, it tells you the door was wider than the words we used to guard it.

attach.answer_text:
Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God — we held that as plainly as the men we spent a century fighting held it, and in the same Latin words. This matters more than it sounds. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

Your second question we have to hand back to you. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place, for our sins? Nobody among us wrote that down, for or against. Our whole surviving argument is about one thing — whose hand may give what the church gives — and we never turned it toward how the cross saves. We would rather tell you we do not know what we thought than hand you a confident sentence nobody here ever said.

What did we believe about God? Here is where you will find us poorer than you expect. We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors — one book, by one man, whom we silenced. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead.

attach.answer_text:
We never disagreed about doctrine. That is the first thing you need to hear, and it is the strangest. For a hundred years two whole churches stood in every African town reciting the same creed at each other. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God - we held that as plainly as the men we spent a century fighting held it, and in the same Latin words. We were called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. The fight was unbearable precisely because there was no doctrinal difference to point at. Only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

So if you are asking who settled a doctrinal dispute among us, the honest answer is that we had no doctrinal disputes to settle. Our whole surviving argument is about one thing - whose hand may give what the church gives - and we never turned it toward how the cross saves, or whether a baby is born guilty, or what the bread becomes. We put everything we had into the purity question, and we had nothing left over.

What we did argue, inside our own communion, was not doctrine but standing. A council of bishops decided, and among us that was never a formality. Our councils deposed men, restored men, and shut down a rival primate. Three hundred and ten of our bishops sat at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in one sentence, and the same body later took two of the condemned back into office. That is not an advisory board. That is a church governing itself.

You can check almost all of it, which is rarer than you think. The proceedings survive - the acts of the council at Cirta, the sentences from Cebarsussi and Bagai, and above all the transcript of the great conference at Carthage, where an imperial notary took down every word for three days. Read that one and you will see how we thought a case ought to be handled. Our own bishop of Caesarea would not let the court touch the merits until it had settled, in order, the day, the mandate, the persons, and only then the cause. First find out who is in the room and by what warrant. Then argue.

There was one man who did think differently about something that mattered. Tyconius, a layman among us, wrote seven rules for reading scripture. It is the one wholly original work of interpretation we produced. He argued from Scripture that the church is spread across the whole earth, which if true meant we were the ones who had cut ourselves off. Our own bishop at Carthage saw exactly where that led, wrote to him, and told him never to preach it again. He did not recant and did not leave. He went on saying it from inside, and we cut him off, and never took him back. His book outlived us in the hands of the church that beat us.

citation_entries.sentence: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God - we held that as plainly as the men we spent a century fighting held it, and in the same Latin words.
That is a church governing itself.
Then argue.

uncited_claim_sentences: Only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

attach_trail.sentence: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God - we held that as plainly as the men we spent a century fighting held it, and in the same Latin words.
Only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.
That is a church governing itself.
Then argue.

attach.answer_text:
We held one creed with the church we spent a century fighting — Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God — in the same Latin words, without variation. This matters more than it sounds. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

So if you are asking us what we believed about the Godhead, the honest answer is: what the other church believed. We did not produce a separate teaching on the Trinity. We did not argue a different Christology. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about God's own nature. We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors — one book, by one man, whom we silenced.

What we did hold, and held absolutely, was not a different doctrine about God. It was a conviction about whose hand may give what God gives. For what we look to is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient — our own bishop's own words. That is a claim about the minister, not about the nature of the one ministered to. We never wrote a treatise on whether God is merciful or just, wrathful or patient. We wrote that a sacrament from a broken hand is nothing.

Your second question we have to hand back to you plainly. Did Christ die to take our punishment, in our place, for our sins? Nobody among us wrote that down, for or against. Our whole surviving argument is about one thing — whose hand may give what the church gives — and we never turned it toward how the cross saves. We would rather tell you we do not know what we thought than hand you a confident sentence nobody here ever said.

attach.answer_text:
For doubt about the rule we held? Look at two rooms, and you should see both.

In the first, our own founding bishops sat at Cirta and were asked straight out whether any of them had handed over the scriptures. Several said yes. Then one of them turned the question on the man presiding, and the room began to mutter that he was no cleaner than the rest. He took advice and put it to the three men present who had not been accused. Their answer was that a case of this kind should be reserved to the Lord. Sit down, all, he said. Thanks be to God, they answered, and sat. Nobody was condemned. Nobody was cleared. The men who would spend the next century insisting a bishop's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real at all found the question unanswerable about themselves, and stopped.

In the second room, a layman of ours named Tyconius worked out from Scripture that the church is spread across the whole earth - which, if true, meant we were the ones who had cut ourselves off from something real. He was told by our own bishop at Carthage never to preach it again. Tyconius did not recant. He did not go over to the other side either. He kept saying it from inside, and we cut him off, and never took him back. So: was there room? There was room to keep arguing, and no room at all to be right.

But if you are asking whether an ordinary member of ours, on an ordinary evening, could feel nothing and wonder whether it was all a mistake - we cannot tell you. That is not modesty. It is that fear, wavering and quiet leaving are exactly what a record kept by our enemies does not preserve. What survives of our inner weather is vindication and defiance, and it survives because it sits in the martyr texts nobody edited.

attach.answer_text: We held one creed with the church we fought, word for word, and the split was never about God or grace or the bread. It was about one thing: whose hand may give what the church gives. We put everything we had into that, and we had nothing left over. So we wrote no book on whether a baby is born guilty. We wrote none on what the bread becomes. We wrote none on faith set against works. The nearest we can bring you is small. A rich woman used to kiss a martyr's bone before she took the cup, and a deacon told her off for it, and that is how we know we had a cup at all. Our own bishop said what matters is the conscience of the giver. That is a claim about the priest, not about the bread. Take those two and you have all we can honestly hand you. Anything more would be us making it up in a voice that sounds like ours.

attach.answer_text:
We would pass the check where we can point you to a dated document or a stone you can touch. We would fail it wherever we have spoken as though the whole body believed one thing in one way.

Start with what stands. Two complete rival hierarchies, see for see, is not a claim we are guessing at. At Carthage in 411 an imperial notary took the roll: two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops stood up against two hundred and eighty-six of theirs, and the transcript survives. That rebaptism happened, and happened as the defining act, is not in doubt. Imperial law names it, opponents argue against it for pages, our own petition describes it as what we do. That we held a purity doctrine about the minister's hand is equally firm. Petilian's own words, quoted whole by an opponent, state it plainly: what we look to is the conscience of the giver. The Bagai council's condemnation and its later reception of two bishops without repeating the rite — both acts are in the record, and the gap between them is real. The inquiry at Zenophilus in 320 is genuine court record, names and sums intact. And two words cut in stone near Bagai — Deo laudes — are the one thing no hostile hand held before us.

Now where we thin out, and we will not hide it. When we say a person came to believe by walking to one font, we are describing the public threshold every source confirms. When we say almost in the same breath that we do not know what any one of them felt at the water, or prayed at night, we mean it. Not one ordinary member of ours left a page of their own interior life. The voices we do have are bishops, councils, martyrs — the ones whose words were worth preserving to argue with or to read aloud at a grave. So a scholar examining us would rightly say: you can show me the institutional act and the doctrinal claim. You cannot show me the ordinary believer's own experience of either, except where an opponent bothered to record an objection to our practice. That is the cost of a record kept almost entirely by the other side.

And we would not survive a test that asked us to speak for the whole movement as one mind. We have shown you a rule stated absolutely and an exception to it held openly, and no resolution. We cannot tell you what the council at Bagai thought it was doing when it took those two bishops back. We can only show you that it did both things. A rigorous inquiry would say: this is a movement that did not settle its own hardest question, not a movement whose answer you have somehow failed to find.

The baptismal threshold and the purity doctrine would stand. The interior life of the baptized and the theological reflection behind the threshold would not. That is the split a scholar ought to hold.

citation_entries.sentence: Two complete rival hierarchies, see for see, is not a claim we are guessing at.
The inquiry at Zenophilus in 320 is genuine court record, names and sums intact.
Not one ordinary member of ours left a page of their own interior life.
The voices we do have are bishops, councils, martyrs — the ones whose words were worth preserving to argue with or to read aloud at a grave.
You cannot show me the ordinary believer's own experience of either, except where an opponent bothered to record an objection to our practice.
A rigorous inquiry would say: this is a movement that did not settle its own hardest question, not a movement whose answer you have somehow failed to find.

uncited_claim_sentences: Start with what stands.
At Carthage in 411 an imperial notary took the roll: two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops stood up against two hundred and eighty-six of theirs, and the transcript survives.
Imperial law names it, opponents argue against it for pages, our own petition describes it as what we do.
So a scholar examining us would rightly say: you can show me the institutional act and the doctrinal claim.
That is the split a scholar ought to hold.

attach.answer_text:
We were not reading for comfort or for doctrine. We were reading for a test we could apply on a Tuesday, in a street, to two buildings.

Understand the situation and the reading follows. Your town has two bishops. Both recite the same creed. Both call their building the church. One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them — some mark that can be seen from outside.

That is what our own bishop of Caesarea was doing when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse. The world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. In your hands those may be verses about the soul's detachment. In ours they were an identification mark. The true church is the one being hated. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.

You will miss something smaller too. Two words could carry all of this. Where they said thanks to God, we said praise to God — Deo laudes — and we cut it into stone. Nothing separates those phrases in meaning. They separated everything in practice. A great deal of our reading works like that. Not the discovery of a hidden sense, but a plain sentence turned into a badge you could be identified by.

attach.answer_text:
What would you miss? That we were not reading for comfort or for doctrine. We were reading for a test we could apply on a Tuesday, in a street, to two buildings.

Understand the situation and the reading follows. Your town has two bishops. Both recite the same creed. Both call their building the church. One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them - some mark that can be seen from outside.

That is what our own bishop of Caesarea was doing when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. In your hands those may be verses about the soul's detachment. In ours they were an identification mark. The true church is the one being hated. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.

You will miss something smaller too. Two words could carry all of this. Where they said thanks to God, we said praise to God - Deo laudes - and we cut it into stone. Nothing separates those phrases in meaning. They separated everything in practice. A great deal of our reading works like that: not the discovery of a hidden sense, but a plain sentence turned into a badge you could be identified by.

attach.answer_text:
Scripture alone was never our claim, and the thing that proves it is what we actually appealed to when the fight got serious. Our case ran on two legs. One was Scripture. The other was Carthage: eighty-seven African bishops, sitting under Cyprian half a century before there was any quarrel between us, who had already ruled that a sacrament from outside the true church confers nothing. When we argued for washing again the people who came to us from the other communion, we were not producing a novelty from a proof-text. We were standing on an African council and on the bishop who presided at it, and we thought that made us the older party, not the newer one. You can see how much that argument weighed by what it forced out of the other side: they had to answer, in writing, that Cyprian is not a canonical authority and the Scriptures alone are. Nobody has to say that unless the appeal is hurting.

There is a harder reason we would not have said Scripture settles everything. We watched it fail to. For three days at Carthage two churches quoted the same books at each other in front of an imperial judge — wheat and tares against the world that does not know him — and at the end of it every man in the room believed exactly what he had believed at the start. When a text can be held by both parties to a hundred-year quarrel, something besides the text is deciding, and among us that something was this: whose hands, in an unbroken line, may hand the thing on.

And there was a third thing, though it sat differently from the first two. Every year, on the day one of our own died, we gathered at the grave and heard the account of that death read out again. That was not an authority to quote from in argument, the way we quoted Scripture or Cyprian. It was an authority of a different kind: the dead who proved, by dying, that what we held was something worth dying for. A bishop wrote to his own congregation about two of their number tortured to death, whose bodies the proconsul sank in the sea so no one could venerate them — and the sea gave them back. We did not file that with our doctrinal proofs. We read it at the graveside, on the appointed day, and let it form us in the hearing. So: Scripture, yes. Cyprian and the African councils, yes. And the witness of our own dead, not quoted in argument but kept in memory, year after year, at the place where they lie.

attach.answer_text: No. Nobody among us hid underground. The persecutions of our own years did not send us into tunnels. They sent soldiers into our buildings in daylight, under orders, to enforce one church. We read the account of one such day aloud every year: a basilica at Carthage seized, a house of prayer turned into a place of feasting, people clubbed to death where they knelt with their eyes shut, and buried inside the walls because there was nowhere else and nobody to stop it. That is what persecution looked like for us. Not hiding. Being visited.

attach.answer_text:
Leadership among us was established by two things held together: the people's voice and the bishops' council, and neither one alone could settle it. We can show you what that looked like when it went wrong. At Cirta, when Silvanus was being made bishop, the people shouted back — let it be another; hear us, God — and he was made bishop anyway, and a court heard about it years later from a man who said, I myself fought against his being made bishop. So a crowd could be overridden. It could not be ignored.

Our senior bishop sat at Carthage. Donatus held it, then Parmenian, then Primian. Our rival claimed the same see for its own man at the same time. So there were two primates in one city, as there were two bishops in every town.

Bishops held authority, and councils held the bishops. That is the short answer, and the size of it is the part people get wrong. In the summer of 411 an imperial officer had both communions counted in one room, and the roll was read name by name: two hundred and seventy-nine of ours stood up, against two hundred and eighty-six of theirs. That is not a movement. That is one whole church facing another whole church, see for see, down to towns you have never heard of.

A council of bishops decided, and among us that was never a formality. Our councils deposed men, restored men, and shut down a rival primate. Three hundred and ten of our bishops sat at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in one sentence, and the same body later took two of the condemned back into office. That is not an advisory board. That is a church governing itself.

You can check almost all of it, which is rarer than you think. The proceedings survive — the acts of the council at Cirta, the sentences from Cebarsussi and Bagai, and above all the transcript of the great conference at Carthage, where an imperial notary took down every word for three days.

What held us together across distance was ordinary and physical. We met: three hundred and ten of our bishops in one place in one year, and two hundred and seventy-nine of them in another room seventeen years later, gathered from provinces that took weeks to cross. We wrote: bishop to bishop, and bishop to congregation, and enough of those letters were read into a court record for you to see how the network actually worked. And we kept days. On a fixed date, in towns that had no other contact with each other, the same account of the same death was being read aloud at the same time. Each year, on the day a martyr died, we gathered at the grave. The account of the death was read aloud again, or preached. We were not looking back at something finished.

attach.answer_text:
We must hear this question the way it comes to us, not rearrange it into something easier. You are not asking whether we failed anyone - you are asking what we did when we did. So before anything else: yes, we failed people, and the hardest cases are the ones we can document most plainly.

First: the person who stood at the wrong font, in good faith, before they knew there was a difference. Our doctrine held that a hand out of a broken line gives nothing - so what looked like a baptism was never a baptism at all. That person had walked through water, heard words said over them, believed themselves received into the body of Christ, and then discovered, perhaps years later, that we held it had all been nothing. What we offered them was the washing. Not as correction of something they had done wrong - they had done nothing wrong - but as the first true entry into what they thought they had already entered. We did not apologize to them for the years they had lived thinking themselves inside something we said they were outside of. We gave them the water and called it the remedy.

Second: the ones we condemned and then took back. Three hundred and ten of our bishops sat at Bagai and spoke of the breakaway party in language about shipwrecked bodies dashed on rocks, covering the shore, unable to find so much as burial. Then the same council took two of those same condemned bishops back into office without washing them again or ordaining them again. We did not write down what we said to them, if we said anything. We did not record whether we named the harm the condemnation itself had done, or whether we thought there had been any harm to name. What we did was take them back, silently, without the conditions we said everywhere else were absolute.

Third, and here we thin out entirely: the person whose own mind would not go quiet. The one who stood at our font, heard our teaching, walked our streets under imperial pressure, and still felt nothing, or felt wrong, or could not make the conviction take. We cannot tell you what we said to such a person, because nobody among us left a word on it. What a hostile-mediated record does not preserve is exactly this: fear, wavering, the quiet drift back to the other communion. What survives of our inner life is vindication and defiance, because those sit in the martyr texts our enemies never filtered. The rest is silent, and we will not fill the silence with an invented pastoral care.

So the answer is uneven. Where the failure was doctrinal - you were at the wrong font - we said the doctrine plainly and offered the remedy our doctrine prescribed: the water. Where the failure was our own - we cursed you and then wanted you back - we took you back without the conditions we said were absolute, and left no account of how we understood what we had done. And where the failure was quieter - your own heart would not settle - we left nothing at all.

attach.answer_text:
No. Not one that anyone can trace to us. The quarrel outlived the empire that fed it and went on for a century and a half more under new masters, and a bishop of Rome was still writing letters about rebaptism in Numidia nearly three hundred years after our founding. Then the record simply stops. No line runs from us to any communion you could walk into now.

We were a complete church, see for see, with our own bishops, our own basilicas, and our own councils. Two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops stood in one room in 411, against two hundred and eighty-six of theirs. That is not a movement that faded quietly. That is one whole church facing another whole church, down to towns you have never heard of. But what 439 removed was the Roman imperial state as the Catholic-aligned power that adjudicates and coerces. Our whole pattern of refusing imperial legitimacy was defined against that power. The two-party contest itself persisted under Vandal and then Byzantine rule, and it falls silent only after the 590s. Then: nothing.

No continuous line to any present-day communion is documented at any point. This is not a living tradition today. No church now living holds a documented line back to it.

attach.answer_text:
We can walk it through, step by step, and we will give you what the record actually holds at each one — not a single person's memory, but what every soul crossing to us crossed through.

First, you came. That is not ceremony yet — that is the plain fact that had to happen before anything else could. You walked to one basilica and not the other one. In every African town there were two bishops, two buildings, two men who would say the words over you. Which door you approached was already a public act, visible to anyone in the street.

Then you were put in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. If you came to us from the other communion, you had already been through water once, with words said over you and witnesses standing there. We held that nothing whatever had happened, because the hand that did it came out of a broken line. What we look for is the conscience of the giver — the one who gives in holiness — to cleanse that of the recipient. So the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

The washing happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was. Washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose. After that day you were in one church and out of another.

We will not hide what came next. Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here — they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong. What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, one opponent writes, and many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether.

Beyond the washing itself, the ordinary shape of belonging among us is thin. We know people prayed kneeling with their eyes closed, because that is how the account describes them when the soldiers came in. We know there was a chalice, because an enemy wrote down that a rich woman used to kiss a martyr's bone before she took it and was rebuked for it. But we have no order of service, no catechetical instruction, no described meal. We would rather hand you those fragments than a plausible order nobody here ever used.

What we can give you entire is one day repeated. Each year, on the day a martyr died, we gathered at the grave. The account of the death was read aloud again, or preached. We were not looking back at something finished. We were being formed again by it in the hearing. That is how the words came to most of us: aloud, at a graveside, on an anniversary, to people who could not check a single detail and came anyway.

citation_entries.sentence: Then you were put in the water.

uncited_claim_sentences: First, you came.
That is not ceremony yet — that is the plain fact that had to happen before anything else could.
You walked to one basilica and not the other one.
Which door you approached was already a public act, visible to anyone in the street.
If you came to us from the other communion, you had already been through water once, with words said over you and witnesses standing there.
After that day you were in one church and out of another.
Beyond the washing itself, the ordinary shape of belonging among us is thin.
But we have no order of service, no catechetical instruction, no described meal.
